newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CSR blames housing again for profit slump.
newsitem.headline: CSR blames housing again for profit slump.

text.p: Building, sugar and aluminium group CSR Ltd said on Monday the 36 percent fall in net profit for the 1996/97 year ending March 31 waS mainly due to the subdued housing industry and partly to lower sugar and aluminium prices.
However, CSR said its U.S. unit made a record net profit of A$117.7 million or about 37 percent of the total CSR profit.
CSR reported a net profit after abnormals of A$212.2 million for the year to March 31, 1997, compared with A$330.8 million a year earlier.
It said in its Australian construction materials business, volumes were steady in generally depressed markets.
Building materials were hard hit by the housing downturn. Prices and volumes for most products were lower and significant restructuring costs were incurred, it said.
It added building material market share was maintained.

The record results set by CSR America was due to continued strength in its markets and contributions from add-on acquisitions, CSR said. It said its American Aggregates quarrying business is still up for sale.
It said results from timber business were disappointing, reflecting domestic and international market pressures.
Last week, CSR decided to keep its timber business after initially put the operations up for sale through a tender.
In sugar, CSR said its Queensland mills processed a record 14.3 million tonnes of sugarcane, a rise of four percent. Raw sugar output increased 10 percent to 2.1 million tonnes.
CSR said net profit from sugar operations fell to A$53.6 million in 1996/97 from A$64.70 million a year earlier.
Aluminium profits also tumbled. The division reported a pre-abnormal net profit of A$58.3 million for the year, down from A$77.60 million a year earlier.

Managing director Geoff Kells said in a statement that all of CSR's divisions had completed fundamental reviews of their operations which had identified further areas to reduce costs, enhance customer service and rationalise activities.
The group sold A$240 million worth of assets during 1996/97.
Kells said the company's major capital expenditure programme of the past few years was now substantially complete.
Analysts have said CSR has spent about A$2.00 billion on its businesses in Australia, Asia and the U.S. over the past three to four years.
